overview: Six weekly 30–40 minute lessons on digital citizenship for second graders using shared class iPads. No prior knowledge is assumed: each week opens with a Learn It picture story that explains the idea from scratch (what being online means, what private information is, what an ad is), followed by a quick check question. Students then practice with the week’s iPad activities, and the lesson ends with a share-out. Every word on the student pages is read aloud in a recorded voice, so students who are still building reading skills can play independently with headphones.
standard: Aligned to ISTE Student Standard 2 (Digital Citizen) and the K–2 themes taught in most digital citizenship programs: media balance, privacy, communication, safety and digital footprint.
routine: Ask the opening question and show the week’s three vocabulary words.
Play the week’s Learn It story on the projector. Pause on each picture and ask students what they notice. Do the quick check as a class.
Students do Learn It on their own iPad, then the week’s activities (headphones on). Circulate and ask “Why did you choose that?”
Use the discussion questions. Students share one thing they will do this week.
before: iPads charged, with headphones for every student
Keyboards attached and paired on every iPad (Meet the Keyboard, the password maker and Type a Kind Reply use them)
Bookmark or add the site to each iPad’s Home Screen (Share ▸ Add to Home Screen)
Test that sound plays on one iPad (check the silent switch and volume)
Projector or Apple TV ready to play the Learn It story together
Shared iPads: each student taps “New student” on the start screen if badges from someone else are showing. Badges also clear by themselves after an hour.
Printed skills checklist (bottom of this page)
Optional: send the home connection note each week

1.ican: I can take care of my iPad and make responsible choices.
1.hook: Hold up an iPad: How much do you think this cost? Who paid for it? What does a good citizen do with things the whole class shares? (Week 1 has eight activities, so it can stretch over two sessions.)
discuss: What does it mean to be online?
Which part of the iPad takes pictures? When is it OK to use it?
What is one way you take care of our class iPads?
What should the iPad look like when you hand it to the next friend?
How are online rules like real-world rules?
Is fixing a cracked screen a good or a service? Who pays for it?
Why can’t we trade our turn on a class iPad?
Which key would you use to fix a typing mistake?
1.home: Ask your child to show you how they carry an iPad safely, and talk about your family’s device rules.
check: 1A Handles shared iPads responsibly and leaves them ready for the next user
1B Explains what being online and a digital citizen mean
1C Explains producers, consumers, goods and services using our class iPads
1D Finds Space, Return, Delete, Shift and the arrow keys on the keyboard
1.pyp: Fully integrated. Key concepts: Responsibility, Function. Students learn that the iPads were bought with real money and are a shared resource. They practise fair turn-taking as a kind of exchange and refuse to trade class iPad turns for a cookie. Care cards and Walk It to the Cart connect careless use to repair costs. Where Do iPads Come From? covers producers and consumers, goods and services, and opportunity cost (repair money can’t buy books). Learner profile: Principled.

2.ican: I can balance screen time and green time and notice how my body feels.
2.hook: If you had 6 coins to spend on your afternoon, what would you buy? What if the coins were hours of time?
discuss: How does your body feel after a lot of screen time?
What is a green time activity you love?
What can you do when it’s hard to stop?
If you spend an hour on screens, what do you give up?
Why do some apps want you to keep watching?
2.home: Plan a balanced afternoon together using the Screen Time, Green Time idea.
check: 2B Names a strategy for taking a break
2C Plans a time budget that fits must-dos before wants
2.pyp: Fully integrated. Key concepts: Function, Causation. Time is treated as a currency: students spend 6 time coins in Spend My Time Coins and budget hours in Saturday Time Budget (must-dos vs wants, with an autoplay pop-up to stop). They learn that apps earn money from ads when we keep watching, and meet trade-offs (choosing games means giving up fort time). Learner profile: Balanced.

3.ican: I can tell what information is private and keep my password secret.
3.hook: What would you keep in a treasure box? Private information is like treasure.
discuss: What information should we never share online?
What makes a password strong?
Who are the people who can know your password?
Why don’t we save passwords on our class iPads?
If a game is free, what might the company want from you instead?
3.home: Talk about which family information is private, and who your child can tell if a website asks for it.
check: 3B Knows who may know their password
3C Types a password with capitals, a number and a symbol
3.pyp: Key concepts: Connection, Value. Personal information has value, and “free” apps often trade games for data. Money information is for grown-ups only. Learner profile: Principled.

4.ican: I can use kind words online, just like face to face.
4.hook: How can you tell if someone is happy or upset in a message when you can’t see their face?
discuss: Why can messages be easy to misunderstand?
What can you do before you send a message?
What is a kind reply when a friend makes a mistake?
4.home: Write a kind message together to a family member or friend.
check: 4C Types and sends a kind reply using Shift, Space and Return
4.pyp: Key concept: Perspective. Trading in games is an exchange, so fair trades and kind “no thank yous” matter. Learner profile: Caring, Communicators.

5.ican: I can stop, think and tell a trusted adult when something online feels wrong.
5.hook: Have you ever seen a pop-up that said you won something? What did you do?
discuss: What are some things that should make us stop and think online?
How can you tell if something is an ad?
Who are your trusted adults at school and at home?
What is the difference between a need and a want? How do ads try to make us want things?
5.home: Name your child’s trusted adults together, and practice “Stop, Think, Tell.”
5.pyp: Key concepts: Function, Perspective. Needs vs. wants, how ads persuade, game coins cost real money, and budgeting in the Coin Shop. Learner profile: Thinkers.

6.ican: I can leave a digital footprint I am proud of and be an upstander.
6.hook: What kind of footprints do you leave when you walk in the snow or sand? What footprints do you leave online?
discuss: What is a footprint you would be proud of?
What can an upstander do?
Which pledge promise is most important to you, and why?
6.home: Hang up your child’s Digital Citizen certificate and talk about the promises they chose.
6.pyp: Key concept: Causation. Online shopping and browsing leave footprints that stores use to sell to us. Ask before buying anything. Learner profile: Reflective.

checklistKey: I = does it independently · H = does it with help · N = not yet
pyp: Connects to the PYP unit on Money and Exchange (How we organize ourselves). Throughout the six weeks, students meet the idea that online life runs on exchanges: we spend time like money, apps trade free games for our information, game coins cost real money, ads try to turn wants into needs, and fair trades are kind trades. Week 5’s Coin Shop has students buy a shopping list on a pretend-coin budget, avoid wants that break the budget, close a trick ad and ask a grown-up before paying.
